newsitem.title: NORWAY: NORDIC SKIING-OGIWARA BOUNCES BACK TO WIN WORLD TITLE.
newsitem.headline: NORDIC SKIING-OGIWARA BOUNCES BACK TO WIN WORLD TITLE.

text.p: Japanese Kenji Ogiwara proved he was a still a force to be reckoned with by winning gold in the Nordic combined at the Nordic skiing world championships on Sunday.

The 27-year-old from Nagano, warming up for next year's winter Olympics in his home town, resisted Norway's Bjarte Engen Vik to cross the line in front at the end of the second part of the event, the 15-km freestyle cross-country race.
Vik, who dreamed of handing Norway their first title in the 10-day festival which started on Friday, had to settle for second place.

Fabrice Guy of France, who was only 10th after Saturday's ski jumping, had a brilliant race to claim third place and earn his first podium since 1992, the year he won the Olympic title in Albertville.
Victory came as a relief for veteran Ogiwara, who won two Olympic golds and three world championship titles in his career but had not managed a single top three finish this winter.

"Some were saying I was getting old but I just tried to forget what I had already won," he said. "I wanted to start all over again and this win is just what I needed. It's a first step on a road which, I hope, will take me to success in Nagano."
Ogiwara and Vik, second and fourth respectively after the ski jumping, soon caught up overnight leader Samppa Lajunen of Finland, who failed to follow the pace and ended a modest 17th.
Cheered by thousands of noisy fans, Vik briefly enjoyed the lead but with four kilometres to go, Ogiwara overtook him and cruised to victory.
Vik said he had given his all but just could not match the Japanese: "Towards the end, I was really tired," he said. "I had cramps in my arms and legs. Ogiwara was too strong for me today."
Guy, who had never quite recaptured his formidable form of the 1992 season when he won both Olympic gold and the overall World Cup, lifted his arms up in the air as if he had won the race.
"This is so important for me," he said. "It's my first podium since 1992 and didn't even think it was possible. I would have been happy with a place in the top six."
While Norway were still waiting for their first gold medal, Russia won a third thanks to Lyubov Yegorova, who won the 5-km, classical style women's cross-country race.
Inspired by the example of compatriots Alexei Prokurorov and Yelena Vialbe, who won the 30-km and 15-km respectively on Friday, Yegorova clocked a winning time of 13 minutes 29.9 seconds.
Vialbe added a 13th world championship medal to her unique collection with the second time in 13:32.70 while Stefania Belmondo of Italy took bronze in 13:35.00.

Yegorova, who had been struggling to recapture her best form since winning three gold medals at the 1994 Olympics, began to hope for a win when she learned she would start 62nd, like she did when she won gold over the same distance in Lillehammer.
"I thought it was a good sign," she said. "I was feeling in great shape and then I found my skis had been very well prepared. Everything was just perfect."
After Lillehammer, Yegorova retired from competition to give birth to a boy, Viktor. She then experienced health problems and started wondering if she would ever make it back to the top.
"It was particularly difficult because I'm not that young," said the 30-year-old Russian, whose best result this winter was a third place last month before her home fans in Kavagolovo.
Yegorova and Vialbe will go for more in Monday's 10-km race, the second part of a pursuit event which started with Sunday's race.

Belmondo, who said before the start of the 10-day festival that she would search for gold in every competition she would enter, promised she would keep trying in Monday's race, which she will start with a 5.1-second handicap on Yegorova.
"There's only on tactic and that is to start strong and keep going, hoping the two Russian girls will crack," she said. "Or maybe they will celebrate and drink too much vodka. That would help."
